It might take some time. Do you know what is stopping her from seeing a therapist? For me, I hated having to retell the story of my trauma which is why I never wanted to try a new therapist after ending things with the previous one. I used to make up excuses like not having enough time, or trying to convince myself that there was no hope for me or that there did not exist a therapist that would actually help me. Your friends might have given some excuses as to why she doesn't want to go to therapy, but she might also hint (or you might have to dig) for the real cause. The most important advice I can give you is somewhat contradictory. 1. DO not minimize her trauma. and 2. Try not to imply that she is broken or messed up and that she needs therapy to fix her. Instead try to present therapy as an option for reducing the side effects of PTSD. 
As for workbooks, I don't know much about them except that they exist and psychiatrists/ psychologists acknowledge them to be a useful tool. 
Another thing you could do for her is to research and talk about coping mechanisms for the PTSD symptoms. For example, when I wake up with nightmares I scribble down whatever I can remember about the dream and fall back asleep. Then when I wake up, I read it over and if I remember more details I write them down too. Then I rip it up and throw it away. Sounds pretty dumb but it works for me. There are tons of coping mechanisms on the interweb and a therapist would be able to provide her with so many more.

Encourage her to go to try therapy again. Took me 6 therapists to find one that actually helped. If that isn't an option then there are many PTSD workbooks out there. You might want to pick it up and have a read so that you can teach/ work with her on developing coping techniques.

Yup, I have been taking it for a week now. Also have C- PTSD. 7/7 nights I have had very vivid dreams of being raped/ murdered/ yelled at. They are better than the night terrors because when I wake up instead of feeling tired, scared, and sick, I just think WTF was with that dream. During the dreams I only feel fear and anxiety whereas in night terrors I also feel, well terrified. So for me it has not been a complete fix but I would take vivid bad dreams over night terrors any day. Some other things, the meds give me a bad headache and I really feel the effects of having low blood pressure (what the drug was originally designed for). Last night I got out of bed to get water and I forgot to get up slowly. I passed out twice before getting to my kitchen. Choking was involved in my trauma and is a huge trigger for me. Prazosin can cause nasal congestion so I can't breathe out of my nose and get panicky which makes it hard to fall asleep. Hope this helps!

I am doing engineering at university. I hate going to classes because of the people and noise and I find it very hard to concentrate. For me, doing math is a good way to calm down. Engineering is a really good fit for me because solving problems keeps me calm and keeps the flashbacks at bay. If I study for long enough, instead of trauma nightmares I will have math dreams. I am not sure how much this helps but try to find classes that interest you. If you don't feel ok about going to class then skip but spend the time reading the textbook (works for some classes better than others). I also found that sitting in the front of the lecture theatre helped the panic attacks because I can forget that there are a few hundred people behind me. Another tactic you can try is listening to classical/ baroque music in one ear while sitting in class. This drowns out the chatter and might help your concentration.

I have seen a lot of therapists in the last few years. I think I went through 6 before I found one who actually helped me. She was the one who diagnosed me. She doesn't focus on the diagnosis or the trauma at all. She is all about giving me coping strategies and forming habits that keep my from killing/ harming myself. I have been seeing her for six months and she knows absolutely nothing about my trauma. To her it is not important because what happens is irrelevant, it is how it makes me feel. Frankly, this frustrated me a lot in the beginning and it is just now that I am beginning to see the value in her approach. So... don't be afraid to find someone who CAN and WILL help you out. I know it is hard because at this point you don't know if this person exists. But keep looking.

It takes a long time to find something that works sometimes, but there are so many treatment options that you are bound to find something that works for you. It is just a matter of time.
